headline: Age pension rises in August but deeming rates also jump 0.5%, reducing net benefit for part-pensioners
reasoning: The age pension is increasing by approximately $36.80 per fortnight for singles (to $1,237.70) and a combined $55.60 for couples, which Shorte views positively. However, deeming rates are simultaneously rising by 0.5%, with the lower rate moving from 1.25% to 1.75% and the higher rate from 3.25% to 3.75%. This is particularly significant for part-pensioners, as Centrelink uses deeming rates to assume investment returns rather than actual income, meaning those earning above deeming rates on assets like term deposits will be assessed on a higher deemed income, reducing their pension entitlement.
quote: The pension is going up for a single person by about $36.80 to $1237.70 per fortnight, which, you know, it's a good that's a good age pension. In Australia, the couples rate will go up by a combined $55.60. Um, but the the kicking the in the teeth is that for anybody on a part pension. The deeming rates are also jumping by 0.5%. So they're going the lower deeming rate was 1.25. That's going to 1.75. And the higher rates going from 3.25 to 3.75. So Centrelink don't ask you how much you're making on your investments. They assume using these deeming rates.

headline: Tokenisation of real-world assets is accelerating but SMSF investors should proceed cautiously given unresolved compliance and custody questions
reasoning: Shorte notes that tokenisation of a wide range of assets — US shares, managed funds, commercial property, bonds — is expected to accelerate rapidly across sectors. He references early Australian examples such as Duomo and Bricks, which sold partial property ownership to unit holders. The key unresolved issues for SMSF investors are around compliance: proving ownership of tokenised assets, establishing who holds custody, and enabling auditors to verify that the underlying asset exists and is properly owned. Until these issues are resolved, he advises investors to consult their accountant, advisor, and auditor before committing to tokenised investments.
quote: We're being told that everything is going to be tokenized over the next few years. US shares, managed funds, commercial properties, bonds, everything. We've already seen a bit of it in Australia. You know, I don't know if you've ever heard of Duomo or bricks. They used to sell partial amounts of properties to unit holders and but we're going to we're being told this is going to happen and it seems to be moving fairly fast in all sectors. So of course there's some will want to invest. And the question is, you know, it's going to come down to how do you prove compliance wise who who owns the the actual asset that they own the tokens in and who's got the custody of them? How does the auditor prove that, you know, that you own those units or that the actual asset exists? So there's going to be a lot of work needed to be done in the background. And so just say to people, again, don't jump into new stuff without talking to your accountant, advisor and the auditor.

headline: Seven regulatory changes incoming for Australian SMSFs targeting fraud prevention, trustee accountability and fee transparency
reasoning: The Australian government is introducing seven changes to tighten the SMSF space. These include a requirement for a unique bank account per SMSF, a new trustee knowledge test administered by the ATO, an increased supervisory levy of $295 per year charged from inception, mandatory disclosure of the advisor who set up the fund, a separate line in tax returns for advice fees, a contribution to the compensation scheme of last resort (expected ~$20 per fund across 600,000+ funds), and a ban on cold calling by unregistered advisors including through social media platforms. Shorte views most of these positively, particularly the cold calling ban and the education/knowledge test, though notes the difficulty of policing overseas call centres. He also cautions that the supervisory levy is likely to rise over time once introduced.
quote: The ministers come out. They're trying to tighten up on the SMSF space and make sure, you know, trying to prevent some fraud and ensure people are going into them for the right reason. Um, seven really changes that will affect none of them. Absolutely major. But, um, some basic stuff like your SMS has to have a unique bank account... the supervisory levy used to be charged at the end of the first year... they're putting that up in price to $295 a year and doing it from inception... the advice fees now will have its own line in the tax returns... the Smurfs will also now have to contribute towards this compensation scheme of last resort... and then one I really appreciate is that they're going to ban cold calling by none registered advisors.

headline: Liam Shorte warns against dangerous assumption that superannuation will be used to pay off mortgages in retirement, citing Vanguard research showing 48% of Gen Z expect to do so.
reasoning: A Vanguard report found that approximately 48% of Gen Z Australians expect to access their superannuation in retirement to pay off their home loan. Shorte notes he is already seeing people in their 50s gifting money to children for deposits while assuming they can continue working to rebuild their own super. However, research shows 72% of people do not get to choose when they retire due to illness, retrenchment, or family caring responsibilities. He cautions that relying on super to pay off debt is risky because unexpected early retirement could leave individuals dependent on the age pension.
quote: So it was a Vanguard report that came out this this year. And it basically said that a lot of the Gen Z, about 48% of them, expect that they will access their super own retirement to pay off their, their home loan. Um, yes. Look, they're going to have super for their whole lives. So there's the super. Should be a decent amount, but I'm already seeing it already where people in their 50s are are helping their children, giving them some money towards a deposit. They're assuming that they themselves will be able to continue working and to pay that off before retirement and to rebuild the super. But what we're actually finding is that 72% of people don't get the choice of when they retire, or that they get ill, a spouse gets ill, a parent or a child or a grandchild, or they get retrenched. So, you know, you can't bank on the fact when you're 55 plus that you're going to have a job to, to, you know, so you need to be very careful about your planning to use your super to pay off your debt, because you may be left. Um, you know, so just on the age pension for retirement.

headline: SMSF trustees with blended families should review beneficiary nominations as courts expand recognition of step-child relationships after a parent's death
reasoning: Liam Shorte flags that the traditional rule that a stepchild's relationship with a stepparent automatically ends upon the biological parent's death is being challenged by recent complaints tribunal and court decisions. These rulings are increasingly finding that if an ongoing relationship exists, superannuation death benefits may still be passed to stepchildren. SMSF trustees in blended families are therefore urged to review and update their binding death benefit nominations to ensure their intended beneficiaries are correctly captured under the evolving legal framework.
quote: Yeah, just need to be aware that under the long term, the rules are that if you've got a blended family, look, you've got some stepchildren. Um, if the Stepchildren are the children of the mother who dies or father dies the birth mother. Um, that relationship with the stepparent ends in a lot of cases, but what's been happening in the last few years is after the complaints tribunal and some of the court cases, they're leaning more towards saying no, that relationship does not just automatically end. If there's still an ongoing relationship, then there may be an ability to pass money

headline: SMSF residential property borrowing effectively closed off, shifting demand toward commercial property and income-oriented alternatives
reasoning: The new rules prohibit SMSFs from borrowing to buy residential property directly, while commercial property borrowing remains permitted. Liam Shorte notes this is immediately driving clients toward commercial properties and structures such as unit trusts or partnerships where the SMSF holds 50% and members hold the other 50% in their own names. Combined with changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax, there is a strong push toward income-oriented investments, including commercial properties where tenants cover outgoings. He warns that government modelling underestimated the housing supply impact, with estimates now suggesting 12,000–16,000 fewer homes built per year versus the government's original 4,000 figure, potentially backfiring on the broader economy.
quote: So now, as your last caller said, you can no longer borrow to buy residential property directly to an SMSF. So, um, also, as I said, you can still do it for commercial. So straight away. We're seeing people starting to look at commercial properties because some of those tend to be more expensive. What we're seeing is a shift to, um, either unit trusts or a partnership where the SPF made by 50% of the the units are 50% of the property, and the members may buy 50% outside in their own names or in another entity. so people will always find a way to invest in what they feel comfortable with. And with these changes to negative gearing and, um, capital gains tax, uh, there is a real push now for income orientated investments.

headline: Investment bonds gaining appeal as a tax-effective vehicle for mid-career earners and those who have maxed out superannuation
reasoning: Liam Shorte highlights investment bonds as increasingly attractive for people aged 35–45 earning $100,000+, who are now in or approaching the 37–39% marginal tax brackets and find direct share investing in their own name less appealing under the new rules. Investment bonds are taxed internally at a maximum of 30%, with fund managers often achieving materially lower effective rates, and after 10 years withdrawals become fully tax-free. They are also useful for bridging the gap between ages 55 and 60 before superannuation access, funding children's education costs tax-free, and as a home for older investors who have exhausted superannuation contribution caps and face at least 30% CGT outside super.
quote: So for the people we're talking about bonds, there's two sets. There's the people around 35 to 45 and they're earning reasonably good money. Look, I'm not talking huge. I'm talking 100,000 plus. Um, so they're in their 32% tax bracket heading towards the 37, 39. Um, so what they're doing is they want to invest, and now it's no longer really attractive to invest outside in shares in your own name. Um, but they don't want to put it into super because they're not going to be able to touch their super until they're at least 60. So by looking at an investment bond there, they're investing in there where it's taxed internally at a maximum 30%. And often the fund managers and the way it's dealt with in there, they can get that that tax down a lot lower than 30%. And after ten years that becomes fully available tax. No more tax to be paid.

headline: Conservative investors advised to lock in term deposits and annuities above 5% ahead of expected rate cuts, despite RBA uncertainty
reasoning: Liam Shorte observes that across more than 20 institutions he monitors, term deposit rates have already fallen by 0.2–0.4% in the past month, with maximum rates dropping from around 5.6–5.7% to 5.2–5.3%. Annuities are currently available at approximately 5.5–5.7% for five years, which he views as an attractive anchor for conservative investors who typically draw 4–6% per year. He acknowledges significant confusion given the RBA's recent hawkish comments about potential rate increases, and recalls being misled in August last year when two rate cuts were forecast but three rate rises followed. Nevertheless, his view is that locking in above 5% represents a good deal for conservative investors given the current uncertainty.
quote: People are really confused because you heard Michelle Bullock the other day going, they're not going to be afraid to increase rates again if inflation stays out of control. But certainly all the banks that are dealing with are looking at over 20 different institutions, and they've all reduced their term deposit rates in the last month by about 0.2 to 0.4%. So we were getting term deposits up around 5.65.7. Now the maximum was 5.2 to 5.3. So for conservative investors they're looking at locking in maybe some of those term deposits for the two and three years. Also, there is an opportunity at the moment to get annuities at about 5.5 to 5.7 for five years. So that's locking in a return of 5.7% per year for the next five years, which for conservative investors, they're usually attract on spending 4 to 6% a year. That's an ideal sort of cushion or anchor to their portfolio. But for me, if you're conservative locking in above 5%, that's a pretty good deal.

headline: Over-67s with unused concessional contribution carry-forwards should consider using super to offset capital gains before July 2027 rule changes
reasoning: Liam Shorte notes that retirees over 67 who haven't worked for several years may see their myGov account showing no cap space or unused carry-forwards, but unused carry-forward amounts are still accruing. In years where a property or shares are sold generating large capital gains, meeting the work test allows concessional contributions to be made, providing meaningful tax savings. He specifically flags the approaching 1 July 2027 deadline for new capital gains tax rules as a catalyst for action, urging people to consult their tax agent or financial adviser.
quote: In a year where you sell a property, or you sell some shares and you do some work to meet the work test to be able to put some money into super. And don't worry that the allocation, the allowance is still there is just not showing. Talk to your tax agent. Talk to your financial advisor because there's some really good tax savings by putting concessional contributions in in the year that you sell a property or sell some shares with big capital gains. And we know there's a lot of people going to do that before the 1st of July 2027, when the new rules kick in on capital gains.

headline: Retirees risk breaching contribution caps by moving to pension phase too quickly after year-end contributions, especially with Payday Super changes
reasoning: Liam Shorte warns that retirees who maximise concessional contributions near year-end and then immediately roll over to pension phase or transfer to a new fund risk breaching their caps if their employer makes an additional contribution. With Payday Super requiring more frequent super payments, the risk of an unexpected employer contribution is heightened. Once a rollover or transition to pension phase occurs, it is too late to amend the notice of intent to claim a tax deduction. His advice is to wait a couple of days after year-end before claiming the tax deduction and then moving to pension phase.
quote: Some people put extra contributions in to maximise their contributions, but hadn't checked that whether their employer was putting in another contribution, especially with Payday Super coming up, where super had to be paid weekly from now on. So we found that some people had put in, put the money in, claimed their notice of intent for the full amount, and then rolled over to pension or moved to a new fund after the 1st of July. And now they're coming to me and going, oh, we got. We put too much in our employer put in an extra contribution. So, you know, what do we do now? Well, unfortunately, it's too late once you've rolled over or you've moved into pension phase. It's too late to go back and change your notice of intent to claim. So it's a lesson learned for people. Don't try and push things too far. Leave it a couple of days after the end of the year to claim your tax deduction, and then you can move into the pension phase.

headline: Paying an SMSF property deposit personally before the trust account is active risks double stamp duty when the property is eventually transferred back into the fund
reasoning: Liam Shorte warns that paying a property deposit from personal funds before the SMSF bank account is established and the rollover is in place can have severe stamp duty consequences. State revenue offices require that every cent paid for a property comes from the SMSF in order to grant the stamp duty concession when the property is eventually moved from the bare trust back into the fund. If personal funds were used — even if later reimbursed — states can deny the concession and impose double stamp duty, potentially assessed on the much higher property value 10-15 years in the future when the transfer occurs.
quote: The big issue with this is if in the future, you pay off that loan and you want to move the property back into the SMSF from the bare trust and what you may have done stuff compliant for the ATO, the state government's control stamp duty. So when you go to move that property back in, they want to see that every single cent paid for that property has come from the SMSF. Otherwise they won't allow the stamp duty concession. So if you've paid it personally, and even if you've had it reimburse later. The states don't really care about the ATO compliance. They want their money where possible. They don't like these exemptions, so if they can say no, they will. So no. So doing something like that where you're paying for a deposit for a property before the SMS has got its bank account and the rollover is in there. You could be looking at double stamp duty and that's double stamp duty the value when you go to move it later on, it could be 10, 15 years down the track. So it could be a massive hit.

headline: Liam Shorte warns SMSF investors on timing and precision of superannuation contributions heading into the new financial year
reasoning: Shorte advises that SMSF members should not leave contribution planning until the end of the financial year, and should be careful not to exceed contribution limits even by a small margin. He notes that even a $0.20 overage on concessional contributions can trigger that amount being treated as a non-concessional contribution, potentially causing a breach or an unintended bring-forward. He recommends leaving a small buffer rather than pushing right to the limit. The broader message is about disciplined planning and timing rather than trying to stretch the rules.
quote: Don't try and use the rules to the absolute. You know, if the limit this year is 32,500 for concessional contributions, you know, little things like if you put an extra $29,000.20 in and be very careful. We talked about this before that $0.20 the eight year, don't they round everything down so they will treat that extra $0.20 as a non concessional contribution. So if you're doing the full non concessional as well you may end up breaching that rule as well or triggering to bring forward when you didn't want to. So you know just leave a little buffer. It's not going to you know it's not going to change your life dramatically to just be a little bit careful.

headline: Division 296 tax on super balances above $3m may still be preferable to withdrawing funds given higher tax rates outside super
reasoning: Liam Shorte argues that for many people with balances between $3m and $6m in superannuation, it can still be more tax-advantageous to remain in super and pay the additional 15% Division 296 tax than to withdraw funds and pay income tax at approximately 18% (including Medicare levy) on assets held outside super. He illustrates this with an example where someone with $3.5m in super earning 10% faces an effective Division 296 impost of only around 2.92% on the earnings, versus an 18% rate on the same capital if invested outside. He also notes that withdrawing capital exposes it to future capital gains tax rule changes post-2027.
quote: If your income's above 33,000 after age 67, you start paying tax at around 18%, including the Medicare levy. So if you've got, you know, above 3 million in your superannuation, you may find that it's still more tax advantaged to keep that extra money in super and pay the extra 15% Division 206 tax because it's only on the earnings attributable to the balance over 3 million. So I did a quick example where somebody got 3.5 million in super. It earns 10% for the year they take out their pension. But at the time we worked out the earnings on that 350,000. The extra division 206 just worked out a 2.92%, whereas if they'd taken the money out of super, the extra, you know, their balance would have grown to 725,000 above the 3 million. If they'd taken that 725 out and invested it and got the same return, they'd be paying around 18% tax. So don't rush to do things. I spend half my time at the moment modeling these scenarios, and I'm finding the people that balances between 3 and 6 million there tends to be a sweet spot where it's just better off to pay that extra tax rather than taking it outside.
